intro: Today's issue covers grid capacity built ahead of AI load in the UK, a new US federal battery strategy, the EU's first proposed end-of-waste criteria for textile reuse, a new open forest-type map aimed at EUDR due diligence, and a US cabotage crackdown that is squeezing cross-border trucking capacity. Several items are early-stage or partly verified, so watch the caveats.

items.headline: National Grid buys 73 acres in Teesside for a substation of up to 3.2GW to serve a planned AI data center
items.summary: National Grid Electricity Transmission finalized the purchase of about 29.5 hectares (73 acres) at Dorman Point, Teesside, in a land agreement reached in late October 2026. The site is for a new substation expected to provide up to 3.2GW. It would feed a private-wire network serving a nearby AI data center on a former steel site and a battery energy storage system. Balfour Beatty and Steel River Power are linked to delivering the power works. The price and construction timeline were not disclosed.
items.background: In 2025 the UK government identified Teesworks as a prime candidate for a large AI data center complex, and the data center plan was approved in August despite objections. Teesworks is listed as the primary developer. Major US developers, Google among them, have reportedly shown interest, but no operating or investment partner has been finalized. The substation is part of National Grid's Great Grid Upgrade. Local coverage calls it potentially the UK's largest substation, though that is a projection. One locally quoted figure is 1.44GW of contracted capacity with expansion to 3.2GW, but who said it is unverified.
items.problem: The transmission owner is committing land and grid capacity at multi-gigawatt scale before the anchor data center tenant is known. That raises the question of who bears the risk if the load arrives late, arrives smaller than planned, or never arrives. The private-wire design paired with battery storage also blurs the line between shared public network assets and dedicated infrastructure for one customer.
items.where_why: The problem sits at the grid connection and transmission investment stage, which is the slowest link in AI data center siting. Grid builds have long lead times while data center demand is uncertain and lumpy, so capacity gets built speculatively. There is also an information gap: the grid owner cannot observe how firm the eventual tenant's demand is. Land ownership is itself disputed in the coverage: Teesworks versus the publicly owned South Tees Development Corporation.

stakeholders.name: National Grid Electricity Transmission
stakeholders.stake: Earns a regulated return on new assets but risks stranded capacity if the data center underuses the connection.

stakeholders.name: Teesworks / South Tees Development Corporation
stakeholders.stake: Wants to monetize a former steel site and attract a hyperscale tenant; power availability is its main selling point.

stakeholders.name: Prospective data center developers (e.g., Google, reportedly interested)
stakeholders.stake: Want fast, large, firm power; the substation lowers their time-to-power risk.

stakeholders.name: Balfour Beatty and Steel River Power
stakeholders.stake: Construction and private-wire delivery contracts.

stakeholders.name: Local residents and objectors
stakeholders.stake: Land use, environmental impacts and whether regeneration benefits materialize.

hints: Real-options framing: anticipatory grid capacity built for an uncommitted anchor load, with staged expansion (contracted capacity now, more later) as a built-in option.
Compare UK 'AI growth zone' anticipatory build with US large-load tariffs that require collateral or minimum bills from data centers. Who absorbs demand uncertainty under each regime?
Private-wire plus co-located battery storage is a hybrid between regulated network assets and behind-the-meter supply; think about how that changes the contracting and cost-allocation problem.
items.data_leads: NESO Transmission Entry Capacity (TEC) register and connections queue data for UK grid connections; for US comparisons, LBNL 'Queued Up' and state PUC large-load tariff dockets.

related.title: A model for wind farm management with option interactions
related.why: Models interacting expansion and exit real options for an energy site, a natural starting point for thinking about staged substation capacity built ahead of uncertain AI load.

items.headline: DOE unveils national battery strategy targeting an integrated US supply chain by 2030 and launches PNNL-led Battery Manufacturing Accelerator
items.summary: On October 28, 2026, DOE's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation released a national battery strategy. Its goals are a fully integrated domestic battery supply chain by 2030 and US leadership in battery technology and manufacturing by 2035. DOE projects US battery demand across transportation and storage will nearly quadruple, from 179 GWh in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035. DOE also launched BattMan, a manufacturing accelerator led by PNNL with Argonne, Oak Ridge and the National Laboratory of the Rockies plus five universities. No funding amount was disclosed.
items.background: The strategy has six pillars: upstream and midstream supply chain investment, faster lab-to-market commercialization, manufacturing process innovation, grid modernization deployment, international coordination, and workforce. One process problem BattMan targets is electrode production scrap, which Oak Ridge says can reach 40%; part of that work will happen at ORNL's Battery Manufacturing Facility in Tennessee. DOE says the accelerator will apply 'Super Intelligence' (its own term) to production processes. Context: the launch came six days before the midterms, and the EV tax credit expired in 2025.
items.problem: The federal government is signaling an onshoring push for batteries while one major demand-side support, the EV tax credit, has lapsed. The accelerator also has no disclosed budget, and its industry partners are still being recruited. Firms deciding where to site cathode, cell or recycling capacity face mixed signals about policy durability and about how quickly yield improvements will close the cost gap with incumbent overseas producers.
items.where_why: The friction is in midstream manufacturing: electrode coating and cell production, where high scrap rates and process know-how are concentrated abroad. It is also in policy uncertainty, since capacity decisions span a decade while strategies can shift with elections. The demand projection mixes EVs, whose subsidy has ended, with grid storage, which is growing, so the demand forecast that capacity is built against is itself contested.

stakeholders.name: DOE / CMEI and national labs (PNNL, ORNL, Argonne, NLR)
stakeholders.stake: Want to show progress on onshoring and process innovation, and need industry partners to make BattMan relevant.

stakeholders.name: US battery and materials manufacturers
stakeholders.stake: Could gain yield improvements and support, but face uncertain demand and policy durability when committing capex.

stakeholders.name: Grid-storage developers and utilities
stakeholders.stake: Would benefit from secure domestic cell supply for a fast-growing storage market.

stakeholders.name: Foreign incumbent battery suppliers
stakeholders.stake: Risk losing US market share if domestic supply and sourcing preferences scale up.

hints: Learning-curve and yield models: what does cutting electrode scrap from levels as high as 40% imply for the cost gap between domestic and imported cells?
Policy-durability lens: compare firms' battery capacity announcements and cancellations around the 2025 EV credit expiry and this strategy launch.
The strategy pairs a demand projection with supply targets; examine whether storage demand can substitute for weakened EV demand as the anchor for midstream capacity.
items.data_leads: SEC EDGAR 10-K/8-K capex and plant announcements, Census USA Trade Online imports of lithium-ion cells (HS 8507.60), USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries; Benchmark/BNEF if available.
dataset_candidates: NREL North American Lithium-ion Battery Supply Chain Database

related.title: Return to the United States: Impact of Reshoring Announcements and Reshoring Risks on Market Valuation
related.why: Estimates how markets value reshoring announcements and their risks, relevant to how investors may price battery onshoring moves under this strategy.

items.headline: EU Joint Research Centre proposes first EU-wide end-of-waste criteria for textile reuse and remanufacturing
items.summary: The European Commission's Joint Research Centre published a technical report, apparently in late October 2026, proposing EU-wide end-of-waste (EoW) criteria for preparing textile, textile-related and footwear waste for reuse and remanufacturing. It is the first time EU-wide EoW criteria are being developed for preparation for reuse. A companion report (JRC147954) covers mechanical, thermo-mechanical, physical and chemical recycling. These are proposals, not adopted law: a Commission implementing act is still needed, and no timeline has been found.
items.background: The revised Waste Framework Directive (EU 2025/1892) commits the Commission to an implementing act setting textile end-of-waste criteria based on the JRC's work. EU frameworks have so far focused mainly on recycling. Member states currently apply their own national EoW provisions, which the report reviews comparatively. The JRC report covers the sorting, preparing-for-reuse and remanufacturing phases.
items.problem: Without harmonised criteria, operators cannot be sure when a used garment legally stops being 'waste' and can be sold as a product. That uncertainty affects licensing, cross-border shipment and liability. The open questions are where the legal line is drawn and how strict the sorting and quality conditions are, because that determines which reuse and remanufacturing business models are viable.
items.where_why: The friction is at the sorting and grading node of the textile reverse supply chain, where material changes legal status. Regulatory fragmentation across member states creates uncertainty and compliance costs and limits scale and cross-border trade in sorted secondhand textiles. Harmonisation could lower those barriers, but strict criteria could raise sorting costs.

stakeholders.name: Textile sorters and waste-management operators
stakeholders.stake: Want clear, workable criteria that let sorted goods exit waste status without heavy compliance costs.

stakeholders.name: Reuse platforms and remanufacturers
stakeholders.stake: Gain legal certainty and cross-border market access for recovered products.

stakeholders.name: Fashion brands under upcoming textile EPR
stakeholders.stake: Collection and reuse targets become easier to meet if more collected items can legally re-enter markets.

stakeholders.name: European Commission and member-state regulators
stakeholders.stake: Want to replace fragmented national rules without weakening environmental safeguards.

hints: Treat a future implementing act as a staggered natural experiment: member states with strict versus lenient national EoW rules face different-sized shocks.
Reverse-logistics models where a legal status threshold, not just quality, determines the value of a returned item.
Puzzle: how do reuse criteria and recycling criteria interact? Does making reuse easier divert higher-grade feedstock away from recyclers?
items.data_leads: Eurostat waste generation and treatment statistics for textiles, UN Comtrade flows of worn clothing (HS 6309) by member state, and the JRC report's comparative table of national EoW provisions.

related.title: Fast Fashion, Charities, and the Circular Economy: Challenges for Operations Management
related.why: Lays out operations challenges for textile reuse involving fast-fashion take-back, charities and EPR, the exact chain these EoW criteria would regulate.

related.title: Do E‐Waste Laws Create Behavioral Spillovers? Quasi‐Experimental Evidence from California
related.why: Uses a quasi-experimental design to study waste legislation effects, a template for evaluating a harmonised EoW rollout.

items.headline: Google DeepMind, WRI and IIASA release ForTy 2020 global forest-type map; claimed accuracy beats the EU's EUDR baseline, but plantation detection is weak
items.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Research, with the World Resources Institute and IIASA, released Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020 around October 22, 2026. The map classifies every 10x10m patch of land into six forest and land-use types, separating natural forest and timber plantations from tree crops such as oil palm and rubber. On 8,190 expert-checked sites, the developers report 95.5% accuracy for forest versus non-forest, compared with 93.6% for the JRC's EUDR map, and 90.9% versus 87.8% for forest types. Other coverage reports the map identifies only about half of planted forests and tree crops and is wrong for about a third of areas it labels planted forest.
items.background: Under the EU Deforestation Regulation, wood cannot come from primary forest converted to plantation or planted forest after 2020, and tree crops are treated as farmland. Buyers therefore need each plot's land-use history. ForTy follows the partners' 2025 Natural Forests of the World map. Wood Central cites an August 2025 review finding that none of 21 public global maps could distinguish forest from tree crops and agroforestry. The accuracy figures are the developers' own evaluation, with no independent validation seen, and the licence terms were not checked.
items.problem: EUDR due diligence depends on geospatial baselines, and competing maps disagree. The new map is reported to be better on aggregate accuracy but weakest on exactly the classes that matter most, planted forest and tree crops. Firms, auditors and authorities must decide which map to trust. Errors translate into falsely flagging compliant suppliers or clearing non-compliant ones.
items.where_why: The friction is at supplier screening and plot-level verification, where buyers face information asymmetry about upstream land history. Map choice becomes a de facto compliance standard. Free, better maps can cut due-diligence costs, but classification error rates that differ by class and region can shift compliance burdens onto particular origins and smallholders.

stakeholders.name: EU importers of timber, palm, rubber and other EUDR commodities
stakeholders.stake: Want cheap, defensible screening tools that reduce compliance costs and false positives.

stakeholders.name: European Commission / JRC
stakeholders.stake: Its own baseline map is now benchmarked against a private alternative, which raises questions about the official reference.

stakeholders.name: Producers and smallholders in sourcing countries
stakeholders.stake: Misclassification could exclude them from EU markets or force costly proof of compliance.

stakeholders.name: Google DeepMind, WRI, IIASA
stakeholders.stake: Want adoption of their open data as the de facto deforestation baseline.

hints: Information-asymmetry and screening models: how does a buyer's choice of classifier, with class-specific error rates, change which suppliers get dropped?
Compare map disagreement across sourcing regions as a source of variation in effective compliance burden, a possible lens on supplier exit or trade diversion.
Puzzle: aggregate accuracy improves while accuracy on the regulation-relevant classes stays poor. What metric should regulators actually use to accept a map?
items.data_leads: ForTy 2020 and the JRC Global Forest Cover 2020 map overlaid with UN Comtrade EU imports of HS 44 (wood), 1511 (palm oil) and 4001 (rubber) by origin; Global Forest Watch tree-cover loss as a cross-check.
dataset_candidates: JRC Global Forest Cover 2020 (EUDR reference map)

related.title: Toward “Omniscient” supply chains: Enabling and incentivizing sustainable operations
related.why: Discusses how better visibility across value chains could enable and incentivize sustainability due diligence, directly relevant to geospatial screening tools for EUDR.

items.headline: Stepped-up US cabotage enforcement removes Mexican drivers and tightens cross-border trucking capacity, Knight-Swift CEO says
items.summary: Knight-Swift CEO Adam Miller told FreightWaves that enforcement of US cabotage restrictions 'is really ramping up' and could further tighten cross-border trucking capacity. He said drivers have lost visas over violations committed at previous carriers. Industry leaders estimated about five months earlier that around 3,200 Mexican drivers had been removed from cross-border operations. Separately, Nuevo León cut a state toll on trucks heading to the Colombia-Solidarity International Bridge by 50%, and Walmart plans a $400M distribution center near San Antonio with 425 jobs (other details unverified).
items.background: Cabotage rules bar foreign carriers and drivers from hauling domestic US loads, which limits how Mexican drivers can be used once they are in the US. Knight-Swift runs more than 26,000 tractors and owns TransMex, whose Mexico fleet runs over 1,100 tractor-trailers. Miller expects Mexico to 'play a bigger role' long term but calls tariffs 'a big unknown'. The Nuevo León toll, introduced April 14, 2025, is charged about 500 meters before the existing bridge tollbooth. The cut does not affect Laredo, Texas tolls, and its start date was not stated.
items.problem: Nearshoring raises demand for cross-border freight just as enforcement removes drivers from the pool. Carriers face visa risk from drivers' past conduct at other firms, which complicates hiring and staffing. Shippers investing in border-adjacent distribution face uncertain cross-border capacity and costs. The capacity impact is currently an executive's view, not official data.
items.where_why: The friction sits at the border handoff in US-Mexico trucking, where regulatory rules decide who may haul what and where. A sudden enforcement shock to labor supply interacts with fixed border infrastructure and local fees such as state tolls. Carriers also cannot fully observe drivers' compliance histories, so enforcement risk spills over across firms.

stakeholders.name: Mexican cross-border drivers
stakeholders.stake: Visas and livelihoods at risk, sometimes for violations at earlier employers.

stakeholders.name: Cross-border carriers (Knight-Swift/TransMex and others)
stakeholders.stake: Shrinking driver pool, compliance costs and capacity constraints, alongside a growing long-run market.

stakeholders.name: US enforcement agencies
stakeholders.stake: Want to uphold cabotage rules and protect domestic trucking markets.

stakeholders.name: Shippers and retailers siting near the border (e.g., Walmart's planned San Antonio DC)
stakeholders.stake: Need reliable, affordable cross-border capacity for nearshored flows.

stakeholders.name: Nuevo León state government
stakeholders.stake: Wants to keep freight routed through its bridges; the toll cut trades revenue for traffic.

hints: Treat the cabotage crackdown as a labor-supply shock and look for effects on border crossing volumes, dwell times and cross-border rates versus domestic lanes.
The Nuevo León toll cut is a small price shock at one bridge; route-choice and substitution across Laredo-area bridges could be a clean comparison.
Puzzle: carriers bear enforcement risk from drivers' past behavior at other firms, an adverse-selection twist on driver screening.
items.data_leads: BTS border crossing entry data (truck crossings by port, monthly), BTS TransBorder freight by port and mode; DAT/SONAR cross-border rates if available; FMCSA carrier census for Mexico-domiciled carriers.
dataset_candidates: FMCSA Motor Carrier Management Information System (MCMIS) carrier census

related.title: Estimating the Operational Impact of Container Inspections at International Ports
related.why: Quantifies how a border inspection mandate affects congestion and throughput at ports, a methodological analog for how enforcement shocks hit cross-border freight flows.

related.title: Adaptation of Foreign Logistics Service Providers' Resources and Capabilities to a New Institutional Environment
related.why: Studies how logistics providers adapt resources and capabilities to a changing institutional environment, relevant to carriers' responses to stricter cabotage enforcement.

thread_to_pull: Three of today's items are about building capacity ahead of uncertain demand under policy risk: National Grid's speculative 3.2GW substation, DOE's battery supply targets set against a nearly fourfold demand projection, and nearshoring distribution centers that depend on cross-border trucking capacity now being cut by enforcement. A related thread links the EU textile end-of-waste criteria and the ForTy map: in both, a technical classification (waste versus product, forest versus tree crop) becomes a de facto market gate. Its error rates and thresholds are an operational lever worth modeling.
